headline: Former Connecticut senator charged in Bridgeport absentee-ballot case
dek: State prosecutors say Dennis Bradley opened a voter’s completed ballot and directed her to change a vote in the August probate-judge primary; he was released and is due in court Oct. 21.
body: Former Connecticut state Sen. Dennis A. Bradley Jr. has been charged in an investigation into the handling of an absentee ballot during Bridgeport’s August Democratic primary, putting a new criminal case at the center of the city’s long-running debate over election safeguards. The [Connecticut Division of Criminal Justice](https://portal.ct.gov/dcj/press-releases/division-of-criminal-justice/10062026bradley?language=en_US) announced the charges Oct. 6 and said Bradley was released on a promise to appear in Bridgeport Superior Court on Oct. 21.

The state says Bradley, 42, of Bridgeport, faces two counts of illegal possession of absentee ballots and envelopes, a charge alleging that he was present when an absentee-ballot applicant executed a ballot, and a charge under Connecticut’s absentee-ballot law. The state’s release identifies the statutes as General Statutes sections 9-140b(d), 9-140b(e) and 9-359. Those are charging documents and allegations, not findings that Bradley committed the conduct. The Division of Criminal Justice explicitly said he is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

The investigation grew out of the Aug. 11 Democratic primary for Bridgeport judge of probate. Incumbent Paul Ganim faced challenger Mark Bradley, Dennis Bradley’s brother. According to the state, a woman contacted Bridgeport police on Aug. 5 and the State Elections Enforcement Commission, or SEEC, on Aug. 6. She alleged that a man she knew as Dennis Bradley came to her apartment, opened an absentee ballot she had already completed, and instructed her to change her vote from Ganim to Mark Bradley. SEEC referred the matter to the Office of the Chief State’s Attorney for further investigation.

The [CT Post’s report](https://www.ctpost.com/news/article/bridgeport-ct-dennis-bradley-ballot-arrest-22465181.php) said Bradley turned himself in at Troop G in Bridgeport after a warrant was signed. His attorney, Darnell Crosland, told the newspaper that Bradley maintains his innocence, called the allegations “paper thin,” and said his client was working as a canvasser for the Bradley for Probate campaign. Crosland said he negotiated the surrender and confirmed the Oct. 21 arraignment date. Bradley could not immediately be reached for comment, the CT Post reported.

WFSB separately reported that the arrest was announced by Chief State’s Attorney Patrick J. Griffin and that Bradley was charged and released. That account also said the case concerns the same primary contest and that investigators received the initial complaint before the SEEC referral. The consistent point across the official release and the independent reports is narrower than the political arguments surrounding the race: prosecutors have filed charges over alleged ballot handling, but the underlying account remains to be tested through the criminal process.

The timing gives the case significance beyond the individuals involved. Connecticut began issuing absentee ballots for the Nov. 3 general election on Oct. 2, according to the [Secretary of the State’s absentee-voting guidance](https://portal.ct.gov/SOTS/Election-Services/Voter-Information/Absentee-Voting). The state says voters can request ballots without a specific excuse under expanded access rules, while campaign workers and others who distribute or handle election materials remain subject to detailed legal requirements. A criminal case involving a former elected official may therefore affect how campaigns, voters and election administrators talk about the boundaries around completed ballots during the final weeks of the 2026 election.

Bridgeport has faced repeated scrutiny over absentee-ballot practices in recent municipal contests. The CT Post reported that Bradley is already scheduled for a Dec. 3 sentencing hearing in a separate federal wire-fraud case tied to his 2018 state Senate campaign. That prior conviction is not proof of the new allegations, and the absentee-ballot charges are a separate proceeding. The immediate next checkpoint is the Oct. 21 court appearance, where the case can move from the arrest and charging stage into formal court proceedings and where the defense can respond to the state’s allegations.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Former Connecticut senator charged in Bridgeport absentee-ballot case
seoDescription: Connecticut prosecutors charged former state Sen. Dennis Bradley in a Bridgeport absentee-ballot investigation tied to the August probate-judge primary.
